title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E410 recasts the theory of flexible and elastic lines in terms of internal force components. At each element Mm there is a tangential force T (tension) and a normal force V (shear). The bending moment is A dphi/ds, where A is the flexural rigidity and phi is the tangent angle. With no distributed loads (p = q = 0) the equilibrium equations of the previous page are (I) dT + V dphi = 0, (II) dV - T dphi = 0 and (III) V = A phi'' (ds constant).

On the previous page Euler eliminated dphi from (I) and (II) to get T^2 + V^2 = C^2, then V = C sin(phi + D) and T = C cos(phi + D). This page continues that argument. phi is measured from an arbitrary fixed direction, so that direction is chosen to make D = 0, giving V = C sin phi and T = C cos phi. The resultant internal force has constant magnitude C. Modern reading: the contact force n = T t + V nu is constant, n' = 0, and phi is measured from the line of action of n.

§XXX. Combining with (III) gives A phi'' = C sin phi, which is the (inverted) pendulum equation. Multiplying by 2 phi' and integrating gives the energy-type first integral A phi'^2 = B - 2C cos phi. Hence ds = sqrt(A) dphi / sqrt(B - 2C cos phi), an elliptic-integral quadrature of arc length against tangent angle. Since dphi = ds/r, the radius of curvature is r = sqrt(A/(B - 2C cos phi)). At phi = 0 this gives r = sqrt(A/(B - 2C)).

§XXXI. The axis AX is taken so that angle AMX = phi, so dx = ds sin phi and dy = ds cos phi. Then dx = sqrt(A) sin phi dphi / sqrt(B - 2C cos phi). The next page integrates this to x = sqrt(A(B - 2C cos phi))/C + const. That is the classical statement that curvature is linear in the distance from the line of the applied force (Jac. Bernoulli 1694; Euler 1744), and it leads to a quadratic relation between cos phi and x.

Purpose: to show that the new 'genuine principles' (force-component balance plus the moment law) reproduce the classical elastica of the 1744 Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. The first integral, the curvature formula and dx = ds sin phi are all correct.
Minor gap: sign conventions for V and for the orientation of phi are left implicit. Setting D = 0 tacitly fixes phi = 0 along the direction of the constant resultant force.

ideas.what: Elimination of dphi from the force-balance equations gives T^2 + V^2 = C^2: the internal force resultant is constant in magnitude, and its direction defines the reference axis.
ideas.modern_name: Conservation of the contact force n (n' = 0) for an unloaded rod; resultant force as first integral
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E410, 1771) as part of his 'genuine principles'; general rod theory Kirchhoff 1859, Clebsch
ideas.where_published: E410 itself (Novi Comm. Acad. Petrop. 15); discussed by Truesdell 1960, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II 11/2)

ideas.what: Tangent-angle equation A phi'' = C sin phi and its first integral A phi'^2 = B - 2C cos phi.
ideas.modern_name: Elastica equation identical to the pendulum equation; energy first integral (Kirchhoff kinetic analogy)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Kirchhoff 1859 for the explicit kinetic analogy; the elastica itself to Jac. Bernoulli and Euler 1744
ideas.where_published: E410; the elastica content also in E65 (Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I, 1744)

ideas.what: Radius of curvature as a function of tangent angle, r = sqrt(A/(B - 2C cos phi)), and arc-length quadrature ds = sqrt(A) dphi / sqrt(B - 2C cos phi).
ideas.modern_name: Intrinsic (Whewell/Cesàro-type) equation of the elastica; elliptic integral for arc length

ideas.what: Passage to Cartesian coordinates via dx = ds sin phi, leading to curvature linear in x.
ideas.modern_name: Bernoulli–Euler moment law: curvature proportional to distance from the line of force

missed.claim: The equation A phi'' = C sin phi is literally the pendulum equation with arc length as time, and its first integral is the pendulum energy integral. This is Kirchhoff's kinetic analogy (1859) in its planar form. Euler does not remark on the analogy on this page. Historians (Truesdell; Levien's history of the elastica) already note that Euler's equations contain it, so this is not new to specialists.
missed.quote: V=\frac{A\,dd\phi}{ds^2}=C\sin.\phi, sumto ds constante, quae per 2d\phi multiplicata et integrata praebet: \frac{A\,d\phi^2}{ds^2}=B-2C.\cos.\phi
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only as a priority footnote for the kinetic analogy; it is already recognized in the historical literature.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a clean, correct re-derivation of the classical elastica from Euler's force/moment balance laws. The content (constant resultant, pendulum-type equation, curvature formula) is well documented by Truesdell and others, and nothing here appears absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image essentially exactly. The only differences are cosmetic: the printed glyph is a round Φ (rendered \phi in the transcription), and 'cos' lacks its period in the r formula.
